clinicalPearls: Defined by a variable triad of optic nerve hypoplasia, midline brain abnormalities (absent septum pellucidum or corpus callosum) and hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction
Diagnosis requires at least two of the three components, so presentations range from isolated visual impairment to complex endocrine and neurological disease
Optic nerve hypoplasia may be unilateral or bilateral and often causes nystagmus and reduced acuity
Endocrine dysfunction is common and may include growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diabetes insipidus
Rare familial cases are linked to developmental transcription factor genes such as HESX1, but most are sporadic
Neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice and micropenis can be early clues to pituitary failure
Coordinated ophthalmology, endocrinology and neurology care is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Septo-optic dysplasia is a disorder of early forebrain and midline development in which the optic nerves, septum pellucidum, corpus callosum and hypothalamic-pituitary axis form abnormally. Disruption of the developmental programme, occasionally attributable to mutations in transcription factors such as HESX1 but usually of unknown cause, leads to a spectrum of malformations. Hypoplasia of the optic nerves reduces the ganglion cell axon population, midline defects reflect failed commissural and septal development, and hypothalamic-pituitary maldevelopment produces variable anterior and posterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. The heterogeneous phenotype mirrors which structures are most affected.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and pituitary region assessing midline structures
Comprehensive pituitary hormone evaluation and dynamic endocrine testing
OCT and visual evoked potentials for optic nerve assessment
Genetic testing where a familial or syndromic pattern is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia or adrenal crisis from cortisol deficiency
Diabetes insipidus with hypernatraemia and dehydration
Growth failure and hypothyroidism impairing development
Seizures or developmental regression suggesting extensive brain involvement
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the balance of the three components; visual impairment is usually stable, but timely diagnosis and lifelong hormone replacement are critical to prevent morbidity and mortality from endocrine failure.
pitfalls: Treating optic nerve hypoplasia in isolation and missing life-threatening endocrine deficiency
Assuming a normal septum pellucidum excludes the diagnosis
Delaying hormone replacement in a decompensating infant
Underestimating the neurodevelopmental and hypothalamic components
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Provide lifelong pituitary hormone replacement tailored to identified deficiencies, including hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, desmopressin for diabetes insipidus, and sex steroids at puberty
Recognise and urgently treat neonatal hypoglycaemia and adrenal crisis as presenting emergencies
Offer low-vision support, refractive correction, and orthoptic management of nystagmus for optic nerve hypoplasia
Provide developmental and neurological therapies for associated impairment
Undertake regular endocrine surveillance and monitoring of growth and puberty
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric endocrinology, ophthalmology, and neurology
Give stress-dose corticosteroid cover during intercurrent illness and offer genetic counselling where a familial or HESX1-associated pattern is identified
